offence_severity: Minimum: 3 years rigorous imprisonment, Maximum: 7 years rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: Injuries noted in post-mortem were not grievous, and the cause of death was asphyxiation due to vomit, not directly caused by injuries
number_of_offences: 10 offences charged, 9 upheld under Section 330 of IPC, 1 acquitted (A-10)
motive: To extract information regarding a 'loot' in a hotel
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the cause of death was asphyxiation due to contents of his vomit, hours after the injuries were inflicted, which was an independent reason for cause of death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the evidence of PW-1 (Zarina) had discrepancies, but separated the falsehood from the truth. The medical evidence was considered reliable, indicating that the injuries were not grievous and did not cause death.
trial_duration: Offence: 23.06.1993; Trial judgment: 22.09.1995; High Court decision: 13.12.2007; Supreme Court decision: 04.09.2018
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: R. Basant, S. Nagamuthu, Sr Advs., Shivaji M. Jadhav, Vishnu P., Brij Kishor Sah, Aditya Khanna, P. Parthiban, Nicholas Choudhury, Ms. Astha Deep, A.S. Vairawan, Prashant R. Dahat, Venkateswara Rao Anumolu, Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar, Ms. Suvrna Ganu, Advs. for the appearing parties. Counsel for the State: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquitted some, convicted others; High Court: Acquitted some, upheld conviction under s.330; Supreme Court: Modified sentence under s.330
prosecution_argument: The State sought to press for charges u/s.304 Part-II of IPC, in case s.302 of IPC was not made out. The prosecution argued that the cumulative effect of the injuries caused by the police officers was responsible for the death of the deceased.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the concurrent opinion of the courts below regarding the non-applicability of Section 302 of IPC should not be disturbed. They also pleaded that the accused were merely executing the orders of their superior officer (accused A-1) and that the injuries were not the cause of death.
legal_principle_applied: Causation is an important ingredient to determine whether a person commits culpable homicide. The Court applied the principle of 'take their victim as they find them' and emphasized the distinction between factual and legal causation.
precedent_relied_upon: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415; Mahtab Singh v. State of U.P, (2009) 13 SCC 670; State of M.P. v. Shyamsunder Trivedi (1995) 4 SCC 262; State of West Bengal v. Shew Mangal Singh and Ors. AIR 1981 SC 1917; Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 10 SCC 455; Ganesh v. State of Karnataka (2008) 17 SCC 152; Jayaseelan v. State of Tamil Nadu (2009) 12 SCC 275; State of Rajasthan v. Mohan Lal and Anr. Criminal Appeal No. 959 of 2018; Soman v. State of Kerala (2013) 11 SCC 382; Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 2 SCC 648
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed to reflect the gravity of the crime, the manner in which the crime was committed, and the need for a deterrent effect. The Court found the three-year imprisonment imposed by the Trial Court to be grossly insufficient and disproportionate.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The police officers' conduct reflected pure act of lawlessness and a violation of their primary responsibility to protect and uphold the law. The manner in which the deceased and his family members were taken into custody was found to be highly inappropriate.
other_sentence_order: The sentence of A-2 to A-9 was modified to the maximum imposable period under Section 330 of IPC, i.e., seven years of rigorous imprisonment, while maintaining the fine imposed by the Trial Court.
